There was a memory train that always ran backwards, a plan train that left before it had a timetable, a worry train with too many carriages and a wistful train that carried nothing but wishes. Looking at the drawings, she found it surprisingly hard to be quite so afraid of them any longer.

Signal, the grey station cat, sat on the very edge of the platform as each train went by, his tail wrapped around his paws and his eyes following the carriages from first to last. He watched every one with grave interest, Mr Bell pointed out, and in all his years at Alder Halt he had never once climbed aboard. Ines decided that the cat was the most accomplished watcher she had ever met, though she kept the thought to herself.

She tried it for a few minutes at a time, sitting very still and naming each thought quietly as it pulled in, in the manner of a station announcer. Memory, plan, plan, worry, memory, she said to herself, and now and then a thought came and went so quickly that she could not name it at all. To her surprise, the naming felt less like work than like standing beside the track with a cup of tea.

Then, without warning, a dark carriage rolled in with the words I am a failure painted along its side in tall, tired letters. Ines had ridden that particular train a thousand times, and before she had even decided anything one foot was already on the step. It was familiar, and there is a strange comfort in the familiar, even when it takes you somewhere you would rather not go.

This time she gripped the edge of the bench and stayed exactly where she was, her heart knocking, while the dark carriage stood waiting with its doors open. It remained for perhaps a minute, a long, shabby minute in which she felt every old argument pull at her sleeve. Then, quite calmly, it shut its doors and slid away round the bend, and Ines was left sitting in the sunshine, astonished that nothing had happened.

Mr Bell had witnessed the whole thing from the far end of the platform, leaning on his broom and apparently thinking about nothing at all. When Ines told him what had happened, her words tumbling out, he heard her through and then asked a single question. Did the platform get hurt, he wanted to know, when the dark train came in and stood there so long?

The fast train was due at twenty past two, and Mr Bell, who seldom gave orders, asked Ines to stand behind the yellow line with her feet together. It arrived with a roar that seemed to shake the planks beneath her, a blur of windows and wind that tugged at her hair and flattened her coat against her legs. Then it was gone, the sound dwindling into the distance, and the rails hummed for a few seconds before falling silent.

When the noise had faded, Mr Bell explained the difference between standing on the platform and riding the train, which he seemed to consider the most important difference in the world. From the platform, he said, you can see the whole train, its length, its colour and its speed, whereas from inside you can see only the seat in front of you and the window beside it. Ines, who had spent most of her life in the seat, found the idea both obvious and astonishing.

Ines remembered the morning of the exam with painful clarity: the hall smelling of floor polish, the clock ticking above the door, the paper turned face down on the desk. She had not once watched the thought I am going to fail as it came toward her, she realised, because she had boarded it at the first whistle and ridden it to the very last page. No wonder she remembered nothing of the questions, since she had spent the whole journey looking out of the wrong window.

A yellow line had been painted along the edge of the platform many years ago, and it was a good deal more faded than the rest of the station. In the mind, Mr Bell told her, there is a line like it, and the whole art is to stand just behind it, near enough to see and far enough to stay dry. Nobody, he added, is ever scolded for stepping over it, and everybody is welcome to step back again at any moment.

Mr Bell suggested that Ines try five whole minutes of simple watching, and from a drawer in the ticket office he produced a small kitchen timer shaped like a tomato. She wound it, set it on the bench beside her and was dismayed to find that its ticking was as loud as a cart on a cobbled street. Five minutes, she thought, could not possibly be long, and she settled her hands in her lap with the confidence of a woman who has never tried.

The first minute went beautifully, and Ines felt a small glow of pride at how easily she was watching her thoughts pass. Then a thought about dinner drifted into the station, followed by a thought about whether there would be enough bread, and before she knew it she was seated in the dining car with a fork in her hand. It is remarkable how quietly a train can pull away when nobody is looking at the doors.

By the third minute she was a very long way from the bench, back in the exam hall with the paper before her and the clock ticking above the door. Her hands had turned cold, her heart was racing, and she was rehearsing the answer to question four for the five hundredth time. As far as her body was concerned, it was still spring, and nothing in the sunshine around her had the power to convince it otherwise.

In the fourth minute something small and precise happened, and it was only this: she noticed where she was. The bench was hard under her, a skylark was singing somewhere above the wheat, and her hands, which she had imagined to be icy, were perfectly warm. She felt her way back to the platform as one steps off a moving train, with a little stumble and a great deal of relief.

When the tomato rang, Ines opened her notebook and, with a sinking feeling, counted the marks she had made each time she boarded. There were eleven, which seemed to her a disgraceful number for five minutes, and she felt as discouraged as if she had failed a second exam. It is a very human instinct to turn a lesson into a verdict, and she had been practising it for years.

Mr Bell read the number over her shoulder and, to her surprise, smiled kindly instead of frowning. Eleven times you boarded, he said, but also eleven times you stepped off again, and the stepping off is the whole of the practice. Nobody who sits down to watch ever runs out of trains, he added, but they do get steadily quicker at noticing when the doors have closed behind them.

Halfway through a drowsy afternoon, Ines opened her eyes and burst out laughing, so suddenly that Signal flinched on the platform. Without noticing, she had spent a full twenty minutes on a beach she had visited when she was nine, carefully planning which flavour of ice cream to buy. It seemed an absurd place for a train of thought to end up, and yet she had taken every step of the journey without a single objection.

She confessed the whole beach episode to Mr Bell, fully expecting a gentle sigh of disappointment, or at least a raised eyebrow. Instead he looked delighted, and told her that the instant of noticing was the watcher at work, and that no one had ever found a better way off a train. The moment you see that you are lost, he said, you are no longer entirely lost, which is the oldest and kindest trick in the book.

Mr Bell admitted, with the air of a man revealing a minor crime, that he still boarded about ten trains every hour, and that he had been doing so for forty years. The difference, he said, was that he now stepped off rather sooner than he used to, and with a good deal less fuss. Progress, in his experience, looked less like a staircase than like a person who keeps tripping over the same stone and learns to smile at it.

Ines began to practise in small moments instead of long, serious sittings, which suited her restless nature far better. As she swept the platform or watered the roses, she let her thoughts pass beside the work like passengers walking past a window, and she nodded to them without leaving her task. A broom, it turned out, was an excellent teacher, because it kept one hand busy and left the rest of her free to notice.

At the ticket window Mr Bell took a pile of old tickets that nobody would ever use and cut them with a pair of long scissors into small, neat cards. They were meant for labels, he said, because a label is a way of holding a thing at arm's length, which is exactly where most thoughts are best examined. Ines took the cards as if she had been given a set of very small keys.

On three of the cards Ines wrote planning, worrying and remembering in her very neatest handwriting, as though the thoughts might be impressed by good manners. The next time a thought arrived, she held the right card up in her mind, and she was struck by how quickly the thought seemed to shrink, like a noise that turns out to be the kettle. Giving it a name did not silence it, but it stopped being a stranger shouting in the dark.

Some thoughts proved harder to name than others, so Ines made a fourth card, which she lettered carefully with the word story. It was for those moments when the mind seemed to be inventing events it could not possibly know, filling the gaps in the evidence with confident, colourful and entirely unreliable detail. She was surprised at how often that card came in handy, and how much she had been believing without checking.

Together they pinned the cards in a row along the notice board in the waiting room, between a faded poster about lost luggage and a timetable from a previous decade. Then Mr Bell invented a game in which he tried to guess the label of her thought from the expression on her face. He was right nearly every time, which was embarrassing, and wrong just often enough to make them both laugh until the kettle boiled over.

Naming a thought, Ines was discovering, did not make it vanish at once, and she had not expected it to. What it did was let her see the thought more clearly, as if she had stepped back from a painting that had been pressed against her nose. There was a small, definite relief in that distance, the relief of being a person who has a worry rather than a person who is one.

That night, instead of chasing each thought as it hurried by, Ines named it quietly, laid the card down in her mind and let the train pull out. She still lay awake for a while, because a single afternoon of practice does not undo years of habit, but the stretches of silence between the trains seemed a little longer. When sleep finally came it came gently, like the tide arriving over flat sand, and she did not notice the exact moment it began.

One warm evening Mr Bell led Ines through a gate at the end of the platform and along a narrow path that ran beside the railway. Half hidden under a bank of ferns lay a heap of dark, mossy rocks, and out of the rocks a spring of clear, cold water was bubbling up into a little stone basin. It had clearly been doing so for a very long time, and it showed no sign of being in a hurry.

The water rises day and night, Mr Bell told her, in summer and in frost, and not a single person has ever been paid to pump it. The mind makes thoughts in much the same way, he said, whether we request them or not, and it would be as strange to blame it for that as to blame a spring for being wet. Ines considered this and found that it was oddly comforting to be told that she was not responsible for every drop.

Ines wondered aloud how many thoughts a person has in a single day, expecting a number as exact as a train time. Mr Bell said that nobody really knows, because a thought is hard to define and harder still to count, and that the enormous figures sometimes quoted in newspapers are nothing more than educated guesses. All that anyone can say for certain is that the mind is far busier than we usually notice, and that it does not take holidays.

Ines knelt on the damp moss and pressed her palm flat over the mouth of the spring, as if she meant to put a stop to the whole affair. For a moment the water paused, swelled and then slid out between her fingers on every side, cold and perfectly unbothered. She took her hand away, wet to the wrist, and could not help admiring its good-natured stubbornness, which reminded her uncomfortably of her own.

Next she built a small dam out of flat stones, pressing each one into place with great care, and the spring, without any visible irritation, simply wandered around it. The lesson was not hard to read: to fight the flow of thoughts is to spend the whole evening building walls that the water will politely avoid. The purpose of watching, she began to see, had never been to stop the spring, but to learn how to sit beside it.

What matters, Mr Bell said, is the way we stand beside the water, and he knelt down, cupped his hands and drank a little from the spring. Some of what comes up is clear and useful, he explained, and some is muddy, and a wise person takes what she needs and lets the rest run away down the hill. Ines drank too, and the water tasted of stone and cold air and the particular seriousness of old things.

At ten past six the slow local train drew into the station, exactly on time, as it had done every evening of Mr Bell's working life. Ines, who by now knew its sound from the far end of the valley, felt a small and slightly ridiculous affection for its reliability. Some thoughts, Mr Bell remarked, are just as regular: they arrive at the same hour, with the same luggage, and sit in the same seat.

Ines realised with a smile that she had a six ten thought of her own, a visitor that never missed an appointment. Every evening, as the light turned gold, she began to wonder whether she had locked the little door of her room, and every evening, without fail, the door was locked. The worry was so punctual that she could have set her wristwatch by it, and that, she saw, was rather the point.

Across the field behind the station ran a narrow path, worn into the grass by generations of boots and hooves, and it cut the corner in a perfectly straight line. A thought that repeats, Mr Bell told her, is very like that path, because every time it is walked it becomes a little easier to find in the dark. Nothing is wrong with the path, he said, but it is worth knowing that you are walking it, and that there are other ways across the field.

In her notebook that night Ines drew a clock face and filled the hours around it with the thoughts that came back at the same time every day. The morning ones were mostly plans, the afternoon ones were mostly regrets, and the evening ones, with a quiet punctuality, concerned doors and locks. She laughed aloud when she saw the finished drawing, because it turned out that her restless mind kept a stricter timetable than the railway.

After a restless night Ines set out along the gravel path that circled the station field, her head down and her hands deep in her pockets. She was not really walking so much as being walked, carried round the bend by a mind that had already chosen the route. The wheat rustled on one side and the railway hummed on the other, and neither of them was invited to her thoughts.

In her mind she was back in the exam hall at question four, the one she had been unable to answer, and she saw the blank space beneath it, as white and wide as a snowfield. Her stomach tightened exactly as it had in the spring, as though the body had kept a perfect record of the event and now insisted on reading it aloud. She tried a new answer, then another, but the clock above the door went on ticking in her head and the paper had long since been collected.

On the fence post by the corner Ines had started to place a pebble each time she completed a lap, a habit she could not have explained if anyone had asked. After seven pebbles she had travelled a long way and arrived nowhere at all, and the memory looked exactly as it had on the first round. There is a particular kind of tiredness that comes not from walking far but from walking the same ground.

Mr Bell was waiting at the gate with his hands clasped behind his back, like a man who had been there for some time and did not mind. He asked where she had been, and when Ines said that she had only been walking, he nodded and observed that a loop is a wonderful thing for returning you to the place where you began. The memory of question four, he added gently, had not changed in the slightest, and was not likely to.

That afternoon, with a pot of white paint and a brush, Mr Bell made two small signs on pieces of old board, and he lettered them in the careful capitals of a man used to painting station names. One said help and the other said circle, and he leaned them side by side against the wall of the waiting room to dry. Ines read them twice, suspecting that she was about to be given a rule for life.

Whenever a thought arrives, Mr Bell told her, she may put a single question to it, as a ticket inspector asks for a ticket. Is this thought helping me to act, he said, or is it only going round in a circle? There is no penalty for guessing wrong, and the question itself is worth more than whatever comes back.

Over the course of one long morning Ines held each thought up against the two signs and sorted it, with the solemnity of a customs officer examining luggage. To her surprise the circle pile grew far faster than the other, and some of the thoughts on it were so old that they seemed to know their own way to the pile. It was a little humbling to see how few of her thoughts were doing any work at all.

She did not try to fight the circle thoughts, because fighting them would only have been one more lap of the same field. Instead she let them stand at the carriage doors with their lanterns and their familiar faces, and she declined, politely and quite firmly, to climb in. It was a strange sort of victory, since nothing at all appeared to have been won, except a little more room.

One thought, however, clearly belonged on the help side of the line, and it had been waiting patiently behind the others all week. Ines could write to the college and ask whether she would be permitted to sit the exam a second time, which was the kind of question that leads to an actual answer. She had not dared to look at it directly before, and now that she did, it seemed smaller and far more practical than the dread.

She wrote the question on a card to deal with after supper, and at once the circle thoughts seemed to grow a little quieter, as though they had lost their audience. Standing at the gate of the loop path, with the sun low over the wheat, Ines said the word circle to herself, quite lightly, and turned away from the gravel. She walked back towards the flower beds with the curious feeling of a person who has just stepped out of a revolving door.

The only place on the platform where Ines's phone could find a signal was the corner beside the white clock, and she stood there like a person warming her hands at a very small fire. She held the phone up, as if offering it to the sky, and sent a message to her friend Clara asking how she was and whether she had time to talk. Then she put it away and tried, with only limited success, to forget that it existed at all.

The first hour passed, then the second, then an entire night, and still no reply came, so that the word sent remained beneath her message like a stone dropped into a deep well. Ines checked the screen at breakfast, at the water tap and twice while pretending to read the timetable. The silence was not in itself unusual, since people are busy, but it had a way of echoing.

By the afternoon her mind had begun to tell a story, and it was a remarkably convincing one. Clara was angry with her, or tired of her, or had quietly decided that a friend who fails her exams is more trouble than she is worth. Every small thing seemed to confirm it: the brevity of her last message, the long gap before the one before that, even a smiling photograph Clara had posted a month ago.

With every hour the story grew more elaborate, adding scenery, characters and dialogue as a novelist might. Ines could almost see Clara in a bright café, laughing with other friends and telling them how hopeless Ines had turned out to be, and she could hear the clink of the cups. None of it had been seen or heard by anyone, but the mind, when it is hurt, is a very persuasive director.

At supper Ines pushed her bowl of soup to one side without having tasted a single spoonful, and sat with her chin in her hands. Her stomach had tightened into a stone, and the cause of it, if she was honest, was nothing more than a message that had not yet been answered. Mr Bell, who had said nothing, quietly moved the bread a little closer to her.

After a while Mr Bell put down his spoon and asked her one very quiet question. What do you actually know, he said, and Ines, after a long pause, had to admit that she knew exactly two things: that she had sent a message and that nothing had come back. Everything else, he observed, was scenery that her mind had supplied free of charge, and rather expensive it had turned out to be.

The next morning her phone buzzed in the corner by the clock with a long message from Clara, and Ines read it with her heart in her mouth. Clara's battery had died on the very first day at her grandmother Nana Rosa's house, which stood in a valley with no signal at all, and she had only just managed to find a charger. She was sorry, she wrote, and she had been thinking of Ines every day, and she wanted to hear everything.

Ines laughed out loud and covered her face with both hands, half relieved and wholly embarrassed, while Signal looked up at her with mild disapproval. The entire terrible story had been false from the first word to the last, and she had believed every line of it with perfect confidence. It was the strangest feeling to be proved wrong about something that had felt so completely like knowledge.

Sitting on the bench, Ines added up what the story had cost her, as one might tot up a bill at the end of a meal. It had taken one whole evening, one supper and most of a night's sleep, and in return it had given her nothing but a headache and a growing conviction that she was hard to love. All of that had been paid in full, in advance, for a train that had never actually come into the station.

That evening Ines opened her notebook and wrote a line beneath a small drawing of a train with no passengers. Most of my dramas, she wrote, were never on the timetable at all, and the real trains are usually a good deal less frightening than the ones I imagine. She underlined it twice, and then, because she was learning, she added a smaller line beneath it: but some of them are true, and I will still have to find out which.

That evening Ines opened her notebook, drew a firm line down the middle of a clean page and wrote facts at the top of the left column and story at the top of the right. It looked like the accounts of a very small shop, and she found a strange satisfaction in the neatness of it. If her mind was going to keep inventing things, she thought, it could at least be made to fill in a form.

Mr Bell suggested that she begin with something small and harmless, and she chose the morning train. That it had arrived seven minutes late was a fact, and it went on the left; that the driver must be careless and the passengers furious was a story, and it went on the right. She was embarrassed to see how quickly the right-hand column filled up compared with the left.

A short message arrived from her mother, and it read, in full, call me when you can. Within seconds Ines's mind had supplied a sigh, a frown, a long silence at the other end of the line and the words I am so disappointed in you, none of which were anywhere on the screen. She looked at the little grey bubble and wrote on the left, plainly, that her mother wanted a phone call.

After supper she and Mr Bell played a new game at the ticket window, taking turns to state only facts about the day, and the rules were stricter than either of them had guessed. Opinions, guesses, predictions and even the cheerful little word probably were all strictly forbidden by the rules of the game. They were both surprised at how short the list of true things turned out to be, and at how much lighter the day felt without the rest.

Then Ines picked up her pen and, with some reluctance, wrote the hardest line of all. Under facts she put I failed the exam, and under story she put I am stupid and my future is over, and she stared at the two sentences sitting side by side like strangers on a train. One was a piece of information, and the other was a verdict, and it was astonishing how much they had been allowed to blur together.

Seeing the two lines side by side stung, and her eyes filled with tears before she could stop them. She did not tear out the page, and Mr Bell, sitting quietly opposite, told her that a sting is permitted and that it only means she cares about something. For a few minutes neither of them spoke, and the lamp swung slowly overhead, and the tears were allowed to be tears.

A nervous commuter named Tomas arrived on the platform and began to check his watch every few seconds, as though the hands might be persuaded to hurry. He tapped his foot, muttered about the delay and stared up the track with the intensity of a man trying to pull a train in by looking at it. Ines recognised him at once, because she had been that man for most of her life.

Beside him a small child squatted on the warm concrete and studied the pigeons with total, unhurried attention, as if nothing in the world could be more interesting than a bird pecking at a crumb. The same late train would carry them both to the same town, and one of them was waiting while the other was simply being there. The difference, Ines thought, lay not in the train but in what each of them was doing with the minutes.

Ines began to see that thoughts are not good or bad in themselves, any more than weather is good or bad, though it may be convenient or inconvenient. It is the judging that adds a second train, a noisy and self-important one, which pulls in behind the first and announces that she should not be thinking this at all. Most of her suffering, she suspected, came less from the thoughts than from the commentary on the thoughts.

The next day she tried to watch a thought pass without awarding it any marks, which proved harder than it sounded, like trying not to think of a white bear. A thought about her mother drifted in, grey and a little heavy, and for a few seconds Ines let it be only that: a thought, shaped like a cloud, moving across a wide sky. Then the judge arrived, as the judge always did, but this time she noticed the gavel, and smiled.

One grey morning Ines woke with a heaviness she knew well, as though a cold stone had been placed on her chest while she slept. Rain tapped at the window, and before she had even put her feet on the floor she sensed, with the certainty of an old sailor, that a particular train was on its way. It was the kind of day on which the sky and the mind seem to have agreed upon the same colour.

She reached for all her usual tools in turn, and one after another they failed to work. The labels felt like scraps of paper, the breathing felt like a chore, and even the memory of Mr Bell's kind question seemed to bounce off her as a pebble bounces off a wall. It was a discouraging discovery that the practice, which had felt so solid a week earlier, could turn to mist on the wrong morning.

At noon Mr Bell announced, without any particular emphasis, that a goods train would pass through the station without stopping. It was a long, black and very slow one, and Ines could hear it groaning towards Alder Halt while it was still a mile or more away, like a great animal dragging its feet. She had the odd and unwelcome feeling that she knew exactly what it was carrying.

As the first wagon crawled past the platform, Ines read the words painted along its side in tall, peeling letters: I am no good. Wagon after wagon followed it, each one weighed down with another memory of a time when she had failed, or blushed, or been ashamed, and there seemed to be no end to the line. The sheer length of the train was part of its argument, since a thing that goes on for so long must surely be true.

She felt the old tug in her chest, the practised pull to climb on and ride, and her whole body leaned towards it like a plant towards a window. Everything in her history was ready to explain why this was no ordinary thought but the one that told the truth about her at last. It would have been so easy, and so familiar, and so completely, bone-deeply exhausting, like a coat she had worn for years.

Ines took a card from her pocket, held it against her knee and whispered the word written on it: story. She could not be certain that the thought was false, and she did not pretend to be, but she knew that a thought, however loud and however long, is not the same thing as a fact. The word felt very small against the enormous train, and yet it was exactly the right size to hold on to.

She did not climb aboard, although every part of her wanted to, and she was surprised to find that this was a physical act, like holding a heavy door shut against the wind. Her hands trembled a little, the thought went on shouting at full volume, and the tears gathered, but she stayed on the bench and went on watching. It was not a triumph, it was merely a decision, repeated from one moment to the next, for as long as the wagons lasted.

At last the final wagon creaked past with a small red lamp swinging at the back, and the sound of the wheels thinned to a murmur and then to nothing. The rails fell quiet, the rain softened and Ines discovered that her face was wet and that she did not particularly mind. Where the train had been there was only the track, black and shining, running away towards a pale seam of light on the horizon.

Mr Bell appeared with two cups of tea, set one down beside her and sat on the bench, saying nothing at all, which was precisely the right thing to say. After a long while he remarked that dark trains call on everyone sooner or later, even stationmasters, and that they are not evidence of a broken person. They are only weather of a particular kind, he said, and the mistake is to read the forecast as a sentence.

The tea was hot and very sweet, and for the first time that day Ines could feel her hands again. Through a gap in the clouds a bar of sunlight fell across the platform, and the afternoon, which had seemed ruined beyond repair, simply carried on as afternoons do. In the middle of her summer, she understood that the practice was not a shield against the dark trains but a way of surviving their visits with her own two feet still on the ground.

After the dark day Ines began to notice something that she had somehow overlooked for weeks. Between one train and the next, the timetable at Alder Halt left long, empty stretches in which nothing whatever was happening, and the station seemed to breathe out. It was in those stretches, she realised, that the station was most truly itself, and not in the bustle of arrivals.

She began to wonder whether the mind has quiet stretches of its own, hidden between its trains and usually missed because we are watching the next one approach. So she sat very still on the bench, listened to the birds in the hedge and waited for the space that ought to exist between one thought and the next. It was like waiting for a shy animal to come out of a wood, and it required just as much patience.

At first the gaps were tiny, hardly longer than a single breath, and she missed most of them entirely, in the way that one misses a word between two loud ones. But as soon as she stopped straining to find them they seemed to widen, rather as the stars come out in numbers once you stop staring at one. Between a plan and a memory there was a pause as clear and cool as a glass of water, and then the next train came in.

Mr Bell lay back on the bench with his cap tipped over his eyes while Ines described the gaps to him, and for a while she thought he had fallen asleep. They are not empty, he said at last from under the brim, because the platform is in them, and the platform is the part that has been there all along. Ines looked down at the boards under her boots and felt, absurdly, that she was meeting them for the first time.

Awareness is rather like the platform, Mr Bell explained, sitting up and straightening his cap: it is there before the train, while the train stands at the door, and long after the train has gone. The trains change all day, big and small, loud and quiet, welcome and unwelcome, but the platform does not change with them. It simply holds whatever arrives, quietly and without any need to approve of it, and it is never in a hurry for the next one to leave.

Ines patted the warm wood of the bench and looked along the length of the empty platform, turning the idea over as one turns over a stone to see what lives beneath. Every train needs a platform to arrive at, she saw, but the platform has never needed any particular train, and it would still be here if the whole timetable were torn down. The thought was so simple that it felt like a discovery and a relief at the same time.

In her notebook she drew a long, flat platform with a row of tiny trains moving along above it, and she took more care over the drawing than she had taken over anything for months. For the first time the thoughts looked small, almost comical, in their little carriages, while the space around them looked wide and calm and endlessly patient. She propped the page against the window and looked at it for a long time, as one looks at a map of a place one means to visit.

The next morning Ines sat in the sun with her eyes closed and tried, for the length of a few slow breaths, to rest in the platform itself rather than in any of the trains. She found the warmth on her face, the faraway noise of a tractor and the plain, undramatic fact of being here, none of which needed to be thought about in order to exist. It was not a mystical experience, and she was careful not to inflate it, for it was simply a quieter way of being in the same body.

That afternoon she admitted to Mr Bell that she did not really know what awareness was, or whether the word meant anything more than a feeling. He said that he did not know either, and that no one has settled the question, since even scientists who study the brain still disagree about what consciousness is and how it arises. The honest answer, he added with evident pleasure, is that we are using something we cannot yet explain to look at everything else.

That evening Ines swept the platform as three trains arrived and left, and she noticed, between one whistle and the next, that she was not in any of them. They had come and gone as they always did, and she had been here throughout, quietly, like the platform beneath the noise. It was a small observation, but it gave her the first real feeling of having room to live in.

An Express thundered through Alder Halt at full speed, and the wind of its passing lifted Ines's hair, snatched a timetable from the bench and sent it spinning along the platform like a startled bird. Big feelings are rather like that, Mr Bell shouted over the noise: they come in fast, loud and without stopping, and they leave the air full of dust. Then, as suddenly as it had come, the train was a dwindling point in the distance, and the silence rushed back in behind it.

On a hot Thursday a signal failed somewhere down the line, and every train through Alder Halt was delayed by forty minutes. The platform filled with weary, impatient people who sighed at their watches, fanned themselves with newspapers and glared at the empty track as though it had personally let them down. By half past three the mood had grown as dense and sharp as the smell of hot metal.

A red-faced passenger named Mr Falk marched up to the ticket window and began to wave his arms like a man signalling to a ship. He declared that this was the worst-run station in the whole country, that he had a very important meeting and that somebody was going to be held responsible. Since Ines was the only somebody in sight, she received the whole of it, as if she had personally broken the signal with her own hands.

Anger rushed into Ines like an Express train, fast and hot and entirely without invitation, and for a second she thought she might shout back at him with all the volume she had been saving since the spring. Her face burned, her hands began to tremble and a dozen perfectly sharp replies lined up behind her teeth, each one eager to be first. She had not known that so much could happen inside a person in the time it takes to draw a breath.

Instead of answering, she did what Mr Bell had taught her and turned her attention inward, looking for the anger as a doctor might look for the source of a pain. It was a heat spreading across her chest, a tightness in her jaw and a hard knot beneath her ribs, and each of these was easier to bear than the word anger had ever been. Sensations, she found, have edges, whereas a story about being wronged goes on and on without any.

Mr Bell had once told her that a feeling and an action are separate things, and now she saw the gap between them, narrow but quite real, like the gap between the platform and the train. Mr Falk was still shouting, though the sound now seemed to come from the far side of a thick window. She said, quite calmly, that she could not repair the signal but that she could telephone the next station and find out when the next train would arrive.

She made the call, listened carefully and passed the answer on to him with a politeness that surprised them both. Mr Falk stared at her for a long moment, as though a vending machine had unexpectedly said good morning, and then he lowered himself onto the bench and gruffly muttered something that sounded very much like thank you. The next train, when it came, was only twenty minutes away, and he boarded it without another word.

That evening Mr Bell told her what he had noticed over many years at the window. Pushing a feeling away, he said, is like holding a door shut against a gale: it is exhausting, it works for a little while and the wind only seems to grow louder. The effort itself, he added, is often more painful than the feeling it is meant to keep out.

Then he showed her the other way, which was to throw the waiting room door wide open. The wind rushed straight through, rattled the notices on the board, turned over a corner of the timetable and, finding nothing to push against, subsided into a draught and then into stillness. Making room, he said, does not mean liking the wind, for it means letting it pass through without breaking the furniture.

A week later another Express roared through the station, and Ines stood behind the yellow line with the wind on her face and, for once, no fear in her stomach. Anger still visited her now and then, as it visits everyone, but when she made room for it, it passed through the platform and left the boards standing. She was beginning to understand that a feeling is an event in the weather rather than a verdict on the person who is standing in it.

On Saturday a special market train brought crowds of shoppers to Alder Halt, and the sleepy platform was suddenly flooded with baskets, bags, children and the warm smell of bread. Every one of them needed a ticket home, and each of them seemed to need it at the same moment, so that the queue at the little window wound out of the door and halfway to the clock. Ines, who had been trained for six slow trains a day, felt her heart begin to hurry.

In the rush she gave a woman the wrong change and had to call her back across the platform, in front of what felt like half the county. The woman shrugged cheerfully and said it happened to everyone, but Ines slipped behind the pillar beside the ticket office with her face on fire. Her mind was already composing the verdict: careless, slow, unsuited to any job at all.

From behind the pillar she watched the whole noisy crowd go by, braced for the stares she was certain she had earned. But nobody was looking at her at all: they were reading their phones, counting coins, calling to children and arguing happily about whose turn it was to carry the cabbage. She might as well have been a lamp post, and the discovery was both a humiliation and a relief.

Everyone, she realised, was far too absorbed in their own minds to spend any time judging hers, and each of them was carrying a private set of worries and regrets on the way to the market. Mr Bell, who had come to stand beside her, said it was like a crowd of people sitting in one cinema and each watching a different film. It is a great mercy, he added, that we are all so busy with our own picture that nobody has time to review yours.

That night, however, the old habit returned, and Ines stood in front of the small mirror above her washbasin and scolded her reflection with surprising energy. You are so careless, she said, and so slow, and everyone could see it, and it was not a kind voice, nor even a particularly accurate one. If anyone else had spoken to her in that tone she would have asked them to leave the room.

Ines saw that she had begun to treat the practice as an inspection, with herself as the guard, her thoughts as the prisoners and a thick clipboard in her hands. Every time a thought slipped past her and boarded a train, she wrote it down and punished herself for the escape. It was an exhausting job, and the prisoners, as it turned out, were not even guilty of anything.

When Mr Bell heard about it the next morning, he suggested gently that she put down the clipboard. The best watching, he said, is warm and curious, the way a good friend would sit beside you on a bench and keep you company without any lecture. A kind attention does a great deal more good than a stern one, and it is a good deal more pleasant to live with.

He asked how she would speak to Clara if Clara had made the very same mistake with the change, and Ines took a long time to answer. She said at last that she would laugh, give her friend a hug and tell her that it did not matter in the least. Mr Bell nodded slowly and said nothing, which was, as she had learned, a way of letting a thing sink in.

The next day she tried speaking to herself in that same warm voice, silently, in the middle of sweeping the platform. It felt odd and a little theatrical at first, like wearing someone else's coat, but after a few attempts something in her chest began to loosen, as a knot does when it is finally given some slack. She even found herself patting the bench beside her, as if comforting a friend who was having a bad day.

Kindness does not mean having no standards, Mr Bell pointed out, for it only means that mistakes are met with help instead of punishment. That afternoon Ines counted the change twice, quite calmly, and when the rush was over and she finally sat down, Signal climbed into her lap and began to purr like a very small engine. She sat there for a long time, being watched without being judged, and found that she could not remember a better kind of company.

One evening Ines asked Mr Bell whether he had invented all this watching himself, and he laughed so heartily that he had to take off his cap and wipe his eyes. He had simply borrowed it, he said, as everyone borrows from everyone, and the borrowing had been going on for a very long time. The best ideas about the mind, in his experience, are never anybody's property and are always somebody's good luck.

He lifted an old book down from the shelf, turned a few of its soft pages and explained that people in many places and in many centuries had turned their attention to their own minds. What she was learning, he said, was a small part of a very long conversation, conducted in many languages and by people who had never met. He seemed to find that deeply cheering, as though the whole of humanity had spent a very long time sitting on the same bench.

In the Buddhist tradition, Mr Bell told her, the practice of watching the breath, the body and the passing thoughts is called mindfulness, and it has been taught by many teachers in many schools. The old instructions speak of seeing each experience clearly as it arises, without grasping at what is pleasant or pushing away what is not. Ines recognised, with the faint thrill of meeting a stranger who turns out to be a cousin, the shape of her own small experiments.

In India, he went on, the writers of yoga and Vedanta described a quiet witness within every person, the one who sees the mind at work without being the mind's work. An old text on yoga describes its aim, in many translations, as the stilling of the movements of the mind, which sounded to Ines like a task for a saint or a fool. Mr Bell said that the word stilling was easy to misread, and that many teachers took it to mean a steadier attention rather than a switch turned off.

Early Christian monks who lived in the deserts of Egypt practised a kind of watchfulness over their thoughts, and they took the work very seriously indeed. One of them, a monk called Evagrius, who lived about sixteen hundred years ago, wrote about catching a thought early, before it grew into a habit or an action. Ines thought of the dark train and its slow, enormous approach, and decided that the monks had probably known it well.

Nearly two thousand years ago a Greek teacher called Epictetus, who had begun his life as a slave, became one of the best-known voices of the Stoic school. He wrote nothing himself, but his students noted down what he said, and the notes have the odd, sharp freshness of a conversation overheard on a train. Ines found it strangely moving that a man who began with so little power over his circumstances had been so interested in the power he did have.

The idea that Ines remembered best was Epictetus's claim that people are disturbed less by events than by the judgments they form about them. It was raining on the platform, and she stood at the window with two cards in her hand, one marked fact and one marked judgment. The rain went on the first card, a wet sheet of grey on the boards, and the ruined afternoon went firmly on the second.

From Rome came the emperor Marcus Aurelius, who lived about nineteen hundred years ago and kept private notes in which he reminded himself to see things as they really are. Mr Bell was careful to add that the traditions explain the watcher in different ways, that they disagree with one another about important matters, and that he had no wish to persuade her of any of them. He asked only that she try the practice and judge it by what it did for her, and he said it in a tone that made the request sound like a friendly dare.

One rainy evening, as they sat in the waiting room with the stove ticking, Mr Bell admitted that he too had once been deeply anxious. Forty years ago he had come to Alder Halt after a hard time in his life, and had slept badly for months, convinced that his mind was an enemy that had moved in with him. He told it in a quiet, matter-of-fact voice, as one reports the weather of another country.

He had begun to sit on the bench, he said, simply because there was nowhere else to go, and he had stayed for forty years. It had not cured him, for there is no cure for being a person, but it had slowly taught him how to live with his own mind without being ruled by it. Ines looked at the worn boards of the seat, polished by so many hours of other people's waiting, and felt that she was sitting in a long and generous line.

At night Ines lay awake in the dark and replayed a conversation from the previous winter, a conversation that had lasted four minutes and had been replayed, by her own estimate, about four hundred times. She remembered every word she had said, and a dozen far better things she could have said instead, delivered with perfect timing and in a voice she had never possessed. The ceiling above her bed seemed to have become a screen, and the film never changed.

Again and again she rewrote the scene, altering a word here and a pause there, like an editor who cannot stop polishing a page that has already been printed. Each new version was cleverer and kinder to her than the last, and none of them altered by a single syllable what had actually been said. It is a strange kind of labour, rehearsing for a performance that closed long ago and will never be staged again.

In the ticket office hung an old photograph of the station, showing a row of men in caps squinting at the camera, and Mr Bell took it down and held it where she could see. The people in it were fixed forever, he said, and the past is exactly like that: you may look at it as long as you like, but you cannot edit it. All you can change is how you hold it, and what you decide to carry from it into today.

A memory, he told her, can teach one useful lesson, and after that it may be put down, like a tool that has finished its job. Ines thought it over for a day and decided that hers was simple and rather small: next time she would say what she meant more slowly, and not be so afraid of silence. When she had named the lesson, the memory felt strangely lighter, as if it had been waiting to be thanked and dismissed.

By daylight the trouble changed direction, and her mind began to look forward instead of back, which is the other way that a mind can leave the present. She stood at the far end of the platform and gazed down the empty track to the distant curve, where, in her imagination, every dreaded train was waiting just out of sight. The sun was warm, a bumblebee was working in the clover, and she was nowhere near any of it.

Her mind had drawn up a whole timetable of disasters, complete with times, platform numbers and passenger lists, and it presented the document with the pride of a clerk who has worked late. Ines studied it carefully and noticed an important detail: not one of these trains had actually arrived. They existed only on paper, and the paper, when she looked closely, was nothing but imagination written in a confident hand.

Mr Bell came to stand beside her at the end of the platform, carrying his lamp, as the evening light began to fade and the hedgerows turned to ink. He said that a great many of the trains we dread never arrive, and that when one does, we often find that we can meet it rather better than we feared. This is not a promise, he added, since nobody can promise the future, but it is what he had seen in forty years of watching real trains and real people.

Planning is useful, Mr Bell said, while worrying is not, and the difference is that a plan has an end and a worry has only an appetite. So Ines sat down at the ticket desk and wrote three clear steps for retaking her exam: write to the college, make a study timetable and begin the first chapter. When she had finished, she looked at the little list and thought that it was remarkably small for something that had caused her so much suffering.

She folded the list in half, put it in the drawer of the ticket desk and slid the drawer shut with a satisfying click. The plan was made, she told herself, and nothing more needed to be done about it tonight, so any further thinking would be mere pacing in the corridor. It was an odd feeling to hand something over to a drawer, like leaving a heavy bag at a station and walking away unburdened.

Later that day the worry came knocking again, loud and entirely sure of itself, and for a moment Ines felt the old pull to open the door and invite it in. Instead she smiled and told it, quite politely, that its business was in the drawer and that she would see to it tomorrow. Then she went back to watering the roses, and the worry, finding no audience, stood on the step for a while and wandered off.

Mrs Dunmore, who ran the little shop in the village of Alder Green, brought the post to the station every Tuesday afternoon, along with the news of the whole valley and the occasional pasty. That day she handed across the ticket window a stiff white envelope sealed with a smudge of gold wax, addressed to the stationmaster in a hand that looked very important. Mr Bell turned it over twice, as one inspects a suspicious egg, and put it on the shelf for later.

The county held a contest each summer for the best-kept country station, and Ines, who had spent many mornings kneeling in the flower beds with a trowel, discovered that she wanted the prize very badly indeed. It was an unexpected sensation, a kind of hunger with a small flag on top, and it made the shelf where the envelope sat seem to glow. All day long her eyes kept travelling there, as a compass needle will always find north.

At closing time Mr Bell opened the envelope slowly, with the care of a man defusing a small bomb, and read the card aloud: Alder Halt had been awarded second prize. Ines felt a quick, sharp disappointment, hot as a stung finger, and then, a moment later, she noticed that she was feeling it, which changed the feeling slightly. It was no longer a verdict about her flower beds but a visitor sitting on the bench, with its hat in its lap.

Wanting, she saw, was one more train, and it arrived whenever something pleasant came within reach, with the cheerful clatter of a thing that has never been refused. It promised that she would be happy once the prize was hers, and it never mentioned that the happiness would also be a train, and would also leave. Outside the window petals from the flower bed drifted along the platform, loosened by a little wind, and nobody asked them to stay.

Mr Bell turned the page of the station calendar and remarked, in passing, that this summer would end too, as every summer does. So would every hard mood and every good one, he added, which was a little sad and a great comfort at the same time, like the sound of a train that is leaving but also arriving somewhere else. Ines looked at the rows of crossed-off days and felt, for the first time, both the lightness and the ache of that.

In the last week of July a heatwave settled over Alder Halt like a lid on a pan, and the rails shimmered, the flowers drooped and even Signal retreated into the deepest shade he could find. Ines woke with a thumping headache that seemed to beat in time with her pulse and to grow a little worse with every glance at the sun. By noon she was sitting on the bench with her head in her hands, certain that she had never in her life felt so awful, and equally certain that she always would.

Pain, Mr Bell told her, comes in two parts, and most of us pay for both. The first part is the sensation itself, a pressure here and a throb there, which is a fact and can be watched like any other. The second part is the story we pour on top, such as this will never end, and I am ruined, and it is all my fault, and it adds nothing but weight.

He also told her, quite firmly, to drink a large glass of water, rest in the shade and take the matter seriously, because watching the mind is no replacement for common sense. A headache that is strong, he said, or that will not go away, should be seen by a doctor, and there was no shame in asking for help with a body any more than with a worry. Ines drank the water, lay down in the shade of the waiting room and felt, within the hour, the first loosening of the pain.

When the platform of her mind felt crowded, Ines returned to her breath, as one returns to a favourite bench in a busy park. She felt the air move in through her nose and out again, the small rise and fall of her ribs, and made no attempt to change any of it. The breath was not special, but it was always there, and it was always happening in the present, which was exactly where she wanted to be.

In the evening, as trains came and went beside her without any particular drama, she counted ten slow breaths on the bench, losing count twice and beginning again without complaint. By the seventh, the crowd in her mind had begun to thin, and by the tenth she felt a quiet that was not empty but spacious, like a hall after the guests have gone. She did not pretend that it would last, and that, strangely, was part of why it felt so safe.

At night Ines lay in bed with the window open and the moon looking in, and she watched her thoughts go by like night trains with small lit windows. Some she let pass without a glance, and some she followed for a moment and then released, and sometimes she drifted into sleep before the last of them had gone. It was not a technique so much as a way of being gentle with the dark.

It did not always work, and Ines gradually learned not to expect that it would, which was itself a small relief. On some nights she lay awake until two or three, listening to the clock, and the harder she tried to sleep the further sleep seemed to retreat, like a shy animal that senses it is being chased. The effort to relax, she discovered, can be the most tiring effort of all, and the least successful.

On those nights she had learned to stop fighting, to get up for a while, drink a glass of water and sit by the open window with a blanket round her shoulders. She did not make the night an enemy, and she did not demand that it should be over, and in that gentle truce the hours passed more quickly than they ever had under siege. Towards dawn a blackbird began to sing, and she realised with surprise that she had been enjoying the dark.

One afternoon, without the slightest warning, a wave of fear broke over Ines at the ticket window, and the ordinary world seemed to slide a few inches to one side. Her heart pounded, her hands shook, her chest felt as tight as a drum and the room appeared to tilt like a ship's deck in a swell. She gripped the edge of the counter, thinking, with total conviction, that something terrible was about to happen to her.

Mr Bell was at her side in a moment, crouching down with a face as calm as a pond, and he did not tell her to calm down. Put your feet flat on the floor, Ines, he said quietly, and feel the boards under your shoes, just that, nothing more. His voice was low and slow, and it reached her like a rope thrown across a gap.

Then he asked her to name five things that she could see, one at a time, and to say them aloud if she liked. She found the clock, the black stove, a bee at the window, Signal's tail and her own two hands, and by the fifth the wave had begun to ebb. It did not vanish at once, but it was no longer the whole sea, and she could breathe around the edges of it.

When she was calm again and the tea had arrived, Mr Bell told her something that he said he would repeat as often as she needed. A feeling that is very strong, or that keeps coming back, deserves the help of a doctor, and watching the mind, however useful, is not a substitute for medical care. Asking for such help, he added, is not a failure of the practice but one of the sensible things the practice teaches you to do.

On Friday Ines took the slow train to Alder Green and visited Dr Hale at the village surgery, a low brick building with a lavender hedge and a very old clock. The doctor listened without hurrying, asked a few careful questions and arranged to see her again in two weeks, and she did not once make Ines feel that she was wasting anybody's time. Back at the station afterwards, Ines felt unexpectedly proud, as though she had passed a small examination of her own.

Back at the ticket desk that evening Ines took out the list from the drawer and read it through twice. Watching, she thought, had never meant doing nothing, and a mind that is clear enough to see its own trains is also clear enough to write a letter. So she began, in careful handwriting, a letter to the college asking whether she might sit the exam again.

She walked to the red post box beside the station and posted the letter before she had time to change her mind, and the clang of the flap sounded like one chapter closing and another opening. Her hands shook a little, and the old voices began to murmur about what the college might say, but she let the answer be a train that had not yet arrived. She went back to the platform and swept it twice, just to feel the broom in her hands.

As the afternoon train pulled away from the platform, a small girl in a red coat was left standing alone beside the bench, with her fists clenched and her face crumpling. She was perhaps six years old, and it was immediately clear that the whole of her world had just rolled out of the station without her. Ines heard the first loud sob from the ticket window and was out of the door before she had decided to move.

Ines's mind began at once to race with questions and fears, each one more dramatic than the last: where was her mother, what if nobody came, what if something terrible had happened. She noticed the racing, as one notices a clock that is suddenly loud, let the questions go by like carriages and knelt on the warm boards until her face was level with the child's. It was the first time that she had used the practice for someone else's sake, and it felt like a muscle she had not known she owned.

She took the small hand in hers and spoke in a voice that was soft, slow and perfectly steady, though she was not at all sure where it had come from. Between sobs the girl explained that her name was Wren, that she had stepped off to look at the pigeons and that when she turned round the train had gone, with her mother still inside it. Ines said that this was a very good place to be lost in, because it had a stationmaster, a cat and almost no way to go wrong.

Mr Bell hurried to the telephone in the ticket office and called the next station down the line, while Ines kept up a flow of cheerful, ordinary conversation about the colour of the girl's coat. A minute later he came out smiling broadly, and announced that a woman in a green hat was at that moment asking everyone there for a girl in a red coat. The whole station seemed to breathe out at once, and even Signal lifted his head from his paws to listen.

The next train back was twenty minutes away, and Ines and Wren filled the time by drawing trains on the backs of old tickets with a stub of pencil. Wren's was purple, with a cat in every window and a smiling face on the front, and Ines drew a long green one with Signal sitting on the roof like a captain. Wren studied the two pictures with the critical eye of an expert and declared that the green one needed more wheels.

When the train drew in, a woman in a green hat flung herself out of the carriage before it had properly stopped and ran along the platform with both arms stretched wide. She lifted Wren clean off the ground and held her so tightly that neither of them could say a word, and for a long moment there was nothing in the world but the two of them. Ines found, rather to her surprise, that she was crying too, quietly and without the slightest embarrassment.

Afterwards she sat down on the bench and noticed that her knees were trembling slightly, as they do after a long run. She was surprised, and a little proud, to realise that she had stayed steady while the child was frightened, and that the old machinery of her own worry had run quietly in the background without once taking the wheel. She thanked the bench silently, as one might thank a friend who had been there all along.

A few days later Ines woke to a flat, grey morning and discovered that nothing inside her was bright. There was no big feeling, no dark train and no peace, only a dull, heavy quietness, like a damp afternoon in a waiting room. She sat on the bench under a low sky, feeling neither good nor bad, and found that this, too, was a state that no one had told her to expect.

She tried her usual tools one after another, and today they seemed to do very little, like keys that fit a different door. Mr Bell, who had been watching her fiddle with them, remarked that watching the mind does not bring peace every day, and that some days are simply messy, like a desk at the end of a long job. The trick, he said, is not to turn a flat day into a failure as well.

Late in the afternoon a pigeon strutted along the rail, puffing out its chest and bobbing its head like a very small general inspecting a very small army. Ines burst out laughing, and kept laughing, partly at the pigeon and partly at her own thoughts, which had been delivering grand and solemn speeches all day to an audience of one bored cat. Humour, she discovered, is also a kind of distance, and it is perhaps the kindest kind, because it is hard to stay frightened of something that has just made you laugh.

On Monday morning the platform filled with commuters, each of them staring straight ahead with the fixed expression of a person who is somewhere else entirely. Ines looked along the line of faces and thought how many busy minds were standing within arm's reach of one another, each one humming privately like a small engine. It struck her as both comical and rather tender, as if she had been shown the inside of a very large clock.

A grumpy man with a heavy bag stood beside a gentle woman who was holding a bunch of late roses, and their faces could hardly have been more different. Ines was nevertheless quite certain that both of them were listening to a voice that nobody else could hear, one muttering about the delay, the other perhaps rehearsing a kind word. Beneath the surface of every ordinary face, she thought, a whole weather system was going on.

Every passenger, she realised, carried a mind like her own, with its own timetable of trains, its own dark carriages and its own pigeons, and she felt the hard edge of her judgments soften a little. Quietly, so that no one noticed, she made a small wish for each of them as they passed: may you be well, may you be at ease. It was a practice she had read about, in the Buddhist tradition, under the name of loving-kindness, and she had always thought it sounded sentimental until she tried it.

Tomas, the nervous commuter, stopped beside her at the ticket window one morning, and for once he was not looking at his watch. You always seem so calm, he said, and Ines laughed out loud and then told him, in a few simple sentences, about the trains and the platform. He listened with his head on one side, as though she were describing a foreign country he might wish to visit.

Later, in the quiet of the waiting room, she tried to wish herself well too, and found it by far the hardest of all. The voice that criticised her was a passenger as well, she decided, with a noisy mind of its own and a long history of being frightened, and it deserved a seat rather than a sentence. When she said the words to herself, it was like putting a warm coat round the shoulders of someone who had been out in the cold for years.

On a warm evening in September Ines and Mr Bell sat side by side on the bench and watched the sun sink behind the wheat, turning the rails to two lines of copper. She had been saving the question for weeks, and she asked it now, quite simply, as one lays down a card. Who is the watcher, really, she said, the one who sees the trains come and go?

Mr Bell was silent for a long time, and the evening seemed to wait politely with him. The old traditions answer that question in different ways, he said at last, and some of the answers are beautiful and some are baffling, and he did not know which of them was right. Scientists, philosophers and teachers have been arguing about it for a very long time, he added, and he saw no reason why a stationmaster should settle the matter by Friday.

He was content not to know, he told her, and had been for forty years, and the not knowing had never once prevented a train from running on time. Ines thought of the question she had been given in the summer, which she had carried about ever since like a stone in her pocket, and discovered that it had worn smooth and become a friendly weight. Some questions, it seemed, are not meant to be answered but to be lived beside.

On Tuesday Mrs Dunmore brought the post, and between a gas bill and a seed catalogue lay a plain white envelope bearing the name of Marlow College. Ines held it in both hands for a full minute, as one holds a bird that might fly, and found that her thoughts had begun to arrive at the speed of an Express. She noticed this, smiled at the absurdity of it and, taking a deep breath, slid her thumb under the flap.

The college would let her sit the exam again in three weeks' time, on the last Monday of September, and Ines read the short, polite letter four times to be sure. Excitement and fear arrived together, like two trains on opposite tracks, and her stomach, as usual, tried to board both of them. She did not pretend to be calm; she stood on the platform of herself and watched them come in, one with a green light and one with a red, and she breathed.

Autumn came early to the valley that year, and the first yellow leaves began to turn over on the platform, scratching along the boards like small, dry animals. Ines studied on the bench between the slow trains, her books open on her knees and Signal asleep across her feet, and found that she could read for twenty minutes without once falling off the page. When her mind wandered, as it did, she brought it back as one calls in a friendly dog.

On her last evening the six ten drew in exactly on time, and Ines and Mr Bell watched it from the bench, as they had done on so many other evenings that she had lost count. She tried to thank him, found that the words were far too small for the purpose, and said them anyway, because a small thank you, truly meant, is better than a large silence. Mr Bell listened with his cap in his hands and said that it had been the best summer he could remember in forty years.

Before she went up to bed he gave her an old paper ticket, soft with age, on which he had written in his careful capitals: Alder Halt to Anywhere. You need not carry the station with you, he said, because the platform goes where you go, and it is a good deal lighter than it looks. Ines folded the ticket into her notebook, between the page of facts and stories and the drawing of the long, flat platform.

In the morning he stood on the platform and waved his cap as her train pulled out, with Signal sitting at his feet like a small grey sentry. The white clock above the door, three minutes slow as ever, shrank to a pale round moon in the window and then disappeared behind a bend in the line. Ines pressed her forehead to the glass, as she had on the day she arrived, and noticed how entirely different it felt.

On the morning of the exam her stomach was a tight knot, and a dark carriage rolled into her mind with the words I will fail painted along its side in the old, familiar letters. This time Ines knew it at once, held up the card that said story and stayed exactly where she was, her feet flat on the floor and her breath moving in and out. The train stood there for a while, shuddering, and then, finding no passenger, it moved on.

In the exam hall the clock ticked above the door, exactly as she remembered, and the smell of floor polish rose to meet her like an old acquaintance. She breathed slowly, felt her feet on the boards and, when she reached question four, read it twice, waited for the gap between two thoughts and began to write. She did not know what the result would be, and for once she found that she could leave the question standing quietly at the back of the room.

Three weeks later a letter lay on the kitchen table beside her cup of tea, and she opened it with hands that were nearly steady. She had passed, and she cried a little and laughed a little and telephoned Clara, who shrieked loudly enough to be heard across the room. Yet the thing she was most grateful for, she realised, was not the pass itself but the discovery that she could stand beside her own mind and keep her footing.

One grey Monday in the city she stood on a crowded underground platform, jostled by briefcases and umbrellas, while trains screamed in and out of the tunnel and a thousand minds hurried past her. She closed her eyes for a moment, let the noise be noise and felt, quite distinctly, the plain boards of herself beneath her feet. The quiet platform was exactly where she had left it, and it had not occurred to it to be anywhere else.

That night she wrote a postcard to Alder Halt, with a picture of a steam train on the front, and she tried to put a whole summer into the space of six lines. She thanked Mr Bell for teaching her to watch, to name what she saw, to tell the facts from the stories, to be kind to the watcher and to ask for help when she needed it. Then she added a postscript for Signal, which was merely a drawing of a fish, as accurately as she could manage it.

That is the heart of it: you can learn to watch your thoughts as they come and go, to meet them with kindness and to step back onto the platform whenever you have been carried away. These are not cures, and they work differently for different people, and nobody can promise you a mind that never talks. This book is general information, not medical advice, so if you feel very low or anxious for a long time, please speak to a doctor or someone you trust.
